classification.difficultyReason: Connects the scaffolded cosine-rule factorizations and semiperimeter substitutions to the squared area rule; the intermediate identities substantially guide the proof.

children.label: a
children.prompt:
Use the cosine rule to show that
$$1+\cos A=\frac{(b+c)^2-a^2}{2bc}$$
and
$$1-\cos A=\frac{a^2-(b-c)^2}{2bc}.$$

spec.description: Unshaded scalene triangle with A upper left, B lower left and C right. Decorative source blue is replaced by house black.
spec.mathematics: AB=c, AC=b, BC=a; no numerical givens or angle marks.
spec.answerVisibility: All labels are permanent question givens.

answer.short:
$$1+\cos A=\frac{(b+c)^2-a^2}{2bc},\qquad 1-\cos A=\frac{a^2-(b-c)^2}{2bc}.$$

Rearrange the cosine rule, then combine each expression over the denominator $2bc$.
answer.worked:
The cosine rule gives
$$\begin{align*}a^2&=b^2+c^2-2bc\cos A,\\\cos A&=\frac{b^2+c^2-a^2}{2bc}.\end{align*}$$
Hence
$$\begin{align*}1+\cos A&=\frac{2bc+b^2+c^2-a^2}{2bc},\\1+\cos A&=\frac{(b+c)^2-a^2}{2bc},\\1-\cos A&=\frac{2bc-b^2-c^2+a^2}{2bc},\\1-\cos A&=\frac{a^2-(b-c)^2}{2bc}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt:
Let $s=\dfrac{a+b+c}{2}$.

Show that
$$1+\cos A=\frac{2s(s-a)}{bc}$$
and
$$1-\cos A=\frac{2(s-b)(s-c)}{bc}.$$

answer.short:
$$1+\cos A=\frac{2s(s-a)}{bc},\qquad 1-\cos A=\frac{2(s-b)(s-c)}{bc}.$$

Factor the numerators in part a and use $2s=a+b+c$.
answer.worked:
Since $2s=a+b+c$,
$$\begin{align*}b+c-a&=2(s-a),\\a-b+c&=2(s-b),\\a+b-c&=2(s-c).\end{align*}$$
Using part a,
$$\begin{align*}1+\cos A&=\frac{(b+c-a)(b+c+a)}{2bc},\\1+\cos A&=\frac{2(s-a)\cdot2s}{2bc},\\1+\cos A&=\frac{2s(s-a)}{bc},\\1-\cos A&=\frac{(a-b+c)(a+b-c)}{2bc},\\1-\cos A&=\frac{2(s-b)\cdot2(s-c)}{2bc},\\1-\cos A&=\frac{2(s-b)(s-c)}{bc}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt:
Use the fact that $(\sin A)^2=1-(\cos A)^2$ to show that the square of the area of $\triangle ABC$ is $s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)$ and deduce Heron’s formula for the area of a triangle:
$$\text{Area}=\sqrt{s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}.$$

answer.short:
$$\text{Area}^2=s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c),\qquad \text{Area}=\sqrt{s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}.$$

Multiply the identities in part b and use $\text{Area}=\tfrac12bc\sin A$.
answer.worked:
Using part b,
$$\begin{align*}\sin^2 A&=(1+\cos A)(1-\cos A),\\\sin^2 A&=\frac{2s(s-a)}{bc}\cdot\frac{2(s-b)(s-c)}{bc},\\\sin^2 A&=\frac{4s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}{b^2c^2}.\end{align*}$$
Let the area be $K$. By the triangle area rule,
$$\begin{align*}K&=\frac12bc\sin A,\\K^2&=\frac14b^2c^2\sin^2 A,\\K^2&=s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c),\\K&=\sqrt{s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}.\end{align*}$$
Take the positive square root because the area is positive.
